scenes.tts: The first film made haploid cells by separating pairs, then copies. Why do those cells carry different allele mixes? Return to the same model. Green chromosomes came from one parent, and orange chromosomes came from the other.
scenes.visual: Hook first. Rebuild the first film's cell, filling 70% of frame height, with one long green-orange homologous pair and one short pair. Four faint haploid outcomes surround it with question marks. Title appears small after the question. Reuse color map exactly: green = chromosome inherited from one parent; orange = chromosome inherited from the other; blue = cell boundary; yellow = current action.
scenes.narration: The first film made haploid cells by separating pairs, then copies. Why do those cells carry different allele mixes? Return to the same model. Green chromosomes came from one parent, and orange chromosomes came from the other.

scenes.tts: Each homolog carries the same genes in matching positions, but its alleles may differ. Copying makes sister chromatids. The homologs then lie side by side during the first division, placing matching D N A regions beside each other.
scenes.caption: Each homolog carries the same genes in matching positions, but its alleles may differ. Copying makes sister chromatids. The homologs then lie side by side during the first division, placing matching DNA regions beside each other.
scenes.visual: Gene-position bands slide onto the long green and orange X-shaped homologs. Matching bands align across the pair. Add allele labels A and a at one band. The short homologous pair waits dimly below. No molecular structure.
scenes.narration: Each homolog carries the same genes in matching positions, but its alleles may differ. Copying makes sister chromatids. The homologs then lie side by side during the first division, placing matching DNA regions beside each other.

scenes.tts: Crossing over exchanges matching pieces between non-sister chromatids of paired homologs. Watch two chromatids cross, break at matching positions, and reconnect. Each changed chromatid now carries green and orange sections, combining alleles from that parent's parents.
scenes.visual: Two non-sister chromatids from the long homologs cross. Yellow cut markers appear at aligned bands. Matching end blocks swap and reconnect. Finish with one green rod tipped orange and one orange rod tipped green. Label the result RECOMBINANT; keep unswapped sisters beside them.
scenes.narration: Crossing over exchanges matching pieces between non-sister chromatids of paired homologs. Watch two chromatids cross, break at matching positions, and reconnect. Each changed chromatid now carries green and orange sections, combining alleles from that parent's parents.

scenes.tts: A second process mixes whole chromosomes. Each homologous pair can face either direction before it separates. One pair's direction does not direct another pair. This is independent assortment: every pair adds another either-or choice.
scenes.visual: Zoom out to three schematic homologous pairs: long, medium, and short. Each green-orange pair sits on a central line with a curved flip arrow. Rotate the medium pair while the long and short pairs stay fixed. Label the panel SCHEMATIC.
scenes.narration: A second process mixes whole chromosomes. Each homologous pair can face either direction before it separates. One pair's direction does not direct another pair. This is independent assortment: every pair adds another either-or choice.

scenes.tts: Look at these paired chromosomes. The long green homolog and short orange homolog face the same pole. If only the short pair flips, which chromosome mix will enter that side? Predict before the arrows move.
scenes.visual: Show only long and short pairs centered. Long green and short orange face a blue target cell on the left. A yellow flip arrow hovers over the short pair. Display WHICH MIX ENTERS LEFT? Keep all chromosomes gently floating.
scenes.narration: Look at these paired chromosomes. The long green homolog and short orange homolog face the same pole. If only the short pair flips, which chromosome mix will enter that side? Predict before the arrows move.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep WHICH MIX ENTERS LEFT? visible. Pulse the short pair's yellow flip arrow slowly without moving the chromosomes yet.

scenes.tts: After the short pair flips, green from both pairs faces the left side. Separation sends that new whole-chromosome mix left. Changing one pair changed the outcome, while every final cell still receives a member of each pair.
scenes.visual: Rotate the short pair so short green faces left. Then animate arrows: long green and short green enter the left target; both orange homologs enter the right target. Place a check beside ONE FROM EACH PAIR. Clear the earlier question.
scenes.narration: After the short pair flips, green from both pairs faces the left side. Separation sends that new whole-chromosome mix left. Changing one pair changed the outcome, while every final cell still receives a member of each pair.

scenes.tts: The count grows by doubling. For each pair, a gamete can receive either homolog. Each added pair doubles the running count across many separate meioses. The screen shows the computed pattern. Crossing over adds more combinations within those whole chromosomes.
scenes.visual: Grow a computed branching tree from one homologous pair to two, then three. On screen only, show 2, 4, 8 beside the levels and label COMPUTED. Overlay recombinant green-orange tips on some terminal chromosome rods. Do not speak the numerals.
scenes.narration: The count grows by doubling. For each pair, a gamete can receive either homolog. Each added pair doubles the running count across many separate meioses. The screen shows the computed pattern. Crossing over adds more combinations within those whole chromosomes.

scenes.tts: The doubling rule counts whole chromosomes and ignores crossing over. It also has a limit for genes. Genes close together on one chromosome tend to travel together. Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.
scenes.visual: Collapse the tree into one long recombinant chromosome. Two nearby gene bands are linked by a short bracket labelled OFTEN TRAVEL TOGETHER. A gene band on a separate chromosome receives its own either-or arrow. Keep the distinction large and centered.
scenes.narration: The doubling rule counts whole chromosomes and ignores crossing over. It also has a limit for genes. Genes close together on one chromosome tend to travel together. Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.

scenes.tts: Meiosis separates pairs, then copies, while crossing over and assortment remix alleles. Crossing over remixes chromosome sections. Assortment remixes whole chromosomes. Fertilization then joins independently made egg and sperm cells, usually giving siblings different combinations.
scenes.visual: Place the two carried actions side by side. Left: a recombinant green-orange chromosome labelled SECTIONS. Right: three pairs routing mixed whole chromosomes into a cell labelled WHOLE CHROMOSOMES. Transform both into an egg and sperm that join; fan out several distinct schematic sibling chromosome mixes.
scenes.narration: Meiosis separates pairs, then copies, while crossing over and assortment remix alleles. Crossing over remixes chromosome sections. Assortment remixes whole chromosomes. Fertilization then joins independently made egg and sperm cells, usually giving siblings different combinations.

scenes.tts: The variation is not a promise that every individual survives. It gives a population more allele combinations. When conditions change, some combinations may work better than others. Diversity raises the chance that some members survive and reproduce; it does not guarantee survival.
scenes.visual: Show a schematic population of varied chromosome-mix icons under one environment. The background shifts color to mark changed conditions. Some icons fade while several different icons remain and reproduce. Label the entire picture SCHEMATIC and keep the word CHANCE, not GUARANTEE.
scenes.narration: The variation is not a promise that every individual survives. It gives a population more allele combinations. When conditions change, some combinations may work better than others. Diversity raises the chance that some members survive and reproduce; it does not guarantee survival.
